blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Large language models (LLMs) provide a flexible interface for recommendation systems. However, their issued rankings require reliable instance-level uncertainty monitoring. In this scenario, comparing uncertainty quantification (UQ) methods becomes challenging because LLM rankers lack a standard item-classification head. Their scores may depend on option labels, prompts, generation procedures, and the available user and item evidence. Existing methods derive uncertainty from different sources and apply it at different stages of the recommendation process. Some methods evaluate an issued ranking, whereas others use uncertainty to change the ranking itself, making direct comparison difficult. Here we introduce a fixed-ranking benchmark which evaluates eight heterogeneous UQ signals as record-level monitors under a shared output contract. We evaluate these signals across four recommendation datasets and two LLM backbones under a shared fixed-ranking protocol. From the results, we draw three main observations. First, UQ method ordering changes across backbones even on the same reference instances. Second, ranking-aligned Top10Mass provides the strongest scalar Error@10 detection in several evaluation conditions, reflecting effective cutoff-aligned monitoring, while its advantage narrows for popularity-tail targets. Third, scalar UQ signals are weak at identifying which control has the larger clipped NDCG@10 difference, whereas source-specific signals, including Perturbation Rank Instability and simple listwise distances, provide stronger paired-control agreement, reflecting their sensitivity to the two controlled evidence sources. These findings motivate us to evaluate ranking-failure detection, robustness across recommendation conditions, and responses to controlled evidence changes as distinct properties of UQ.

blocks.en: 1 Introduction
blocks.zh: 导言

blocks.en:
Large language models (LLMs) provide a flexible interface for recommendation systems by representing user histories, candidate items, and task instructions
in natural language and asking an instruction-tuned model to rank the candidates ( Hou et al., 2024b ) . Such an interface can
support zero-shot or few-shot recommendation without requiring an additional recommendation-specific
prediction head for each domain. In this work, we focus on the LLM-as-reranker setting and use released instruction-tuned backbones directly, without training from scratch or recommendation-specific fine-tuning. However, a fluent and well-formed ranked list may still be unreliable. The relevant item may be missing from the top results
even when the model shows strong confidence. Recent work has begun to consider whether average ranking utility alone is sufficient for evaluating LLM-based recommendation systems ( Jiang et al., 2025 ) . This broader reliability perspective examines whether the model outputs remain trustworthy when the confidence is unreliable, fairness concerns arise, or recommendations are sensitive to preference and presentation biases ( Sah et al., 2026 ; Tang et al., 2026 ) . Practical deployment therefore requires signals that can monitor the reliability of each issued
ranking.

blocks.en:
However, applying uncertainty quantification (UQ) to LLM-based ranking is not
straightforward. Unlike fixed-class prediction, recommendation produces a
user-dependent ranked list whose top- k k outcome is the object being monitored.
An LLM ranker may output candidate labels or the entire ranked list, and its
uncertainty can also be affected by the prompt, the option-label format, the
decoding or sampling procedure, and the user or item evidence provided in the
context. Consequently, different UQ methods may reflect different aspects of the model behavior, which makes their scores difficult to interpret and compare under a common standard. Several kinds of work have approached the uncertainty from different angles. Classical methods focus on the confidence attached to a prediction, either by using predictive probabilities to detect likely errors ( Hendrycks and Gimpel, 2016 ) or by examining whether reported confidence matches the empirical correctness ( Guo et al., 2017 ) . Language-model research extends this idea beyond a single probability score by studying the self-assessed correctness ( Kadavath et al., 2022 ) and consistency across sampled responses ( Wang et al., 2022 ; Kuhn et al., 2023 ) . Moreover, in recommendation, uncertainty has taken on a broader role: it has been used to estimate the recommendation quality ( Li et al., 2025 ) , distinguish recommendation uncertainty from uncertainty of prompts ( Kweon et al., 2025 ) , and support reranking or model optimization ( Xu et al., 2026 ; Fan et al., 2026 ) . These methods are difficult to compare directly because they differ both in
the uncertainty signals they use and in how uncertainty enters the
recommendation process ( Xu et al., 2026 ; Fan et al., 2026 ) . In particular, methods that use uncertainty for
reranking or model optimization also change the recommendation output, making it difficult to separate UQ monitoring quality from changes in the underlying ranking. To isolate monitoring quality, we therefore hold each issued ranking fixed and map every method to the same record-level output. This fixed-ranking design allows different UQ signals to be evaluated on the same recommendation
outcome under a common standard.

blocks.en:
Building on this fixed-ranking design, we construct a benchmark for UQ in LLM-based recommendation. Each 20-candidate base ranking is generated once and remains unchanged during UQ evaluation. Eight heterogeneous UQ signals are compared as
the record-level monitors under a shared output contract. The full Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct evaluation ( Grattafiori et al., 2024 ) spans four
recommendation datasets and four evaluation settings: a full-evidence reference condition (Warm-start), user-history truncation (Sparse-history), controlled candidate item-text ablation (Item-text robustness), and a subset of Warm-start records whose positive items fall in the popularity tail (Tail-target). We also evaluate Qwen3-8B in non-thinking mode ( Qwen Team, 2025 ) on the same 4,000 reference instances to examine whether UQ method ordering is preserved on a second backbone. This comparison is limited to the reference condition and does not establish broad cross-model transfer. The benchmark defines two complementary evaluation tasks. ① Ranking-Failure Detection evaluates whether a UQ score can flag Error@10 cases, where the target item is absent from the fixed top-10 ranking. ② Paired-control response agreement compares matched user-history and item-content interventions for the same base instance and tests whether a method responds more strongly to the source with the larger clipped NDCG@10 difference. Sparse-history and Item-text robustness provide the user-history and item-content controls, respectively.

blocks.en:
Our experiments yield three main observations. First, the relative
effectiveness of UQ monitors is not stable across LLM backbones. Second,
ranking-aligned probability mass provides a strong scalar signal for detecting
ranking failures, but its advantage varies across evaluation conditions and
target-popularity regimes; these results support ranking-aligned monitoring for the corresponding ranking-failure objective. Third, scalar failure detection and paired evidence-response agreement capture different properties of UQ: source-specific signals are better suited to source-specific diagnosis under the clipped paired-control target, with simple non-UQ
ranking distances showing similarly strong agreement. This last finding is limited to the two constructed controls and does not establish
general source attribution. Our contributions are summarized as follows: • We define fixed-ranking UQ monitoring for LLM-based recommendation
and introduce two evaluation tasks: Error@10 detection and paired-control
response agreement for user-history and item-content evidence; • We build an extensive benchmark that compares eight UQ signals
across four datasets. It includes a full Llama evaluation suite and a Qwen
Warm-start replication on the same 4,000 instances under a shared
record-level contract; • We provide practical guidance for evaluating UQ in LLM-based
recommendation: ranking-failure detection and paired-control response agreement
capture distinct properties of UQ, and method robustness should be assessed
across backbones and recommendation conditions because conclusions from a
single reference setting may not generalize.

blocks.en: 2 Related Work
blocks.zh: 2 相关工作

blocks.en: 2.1 LLMs for Recommendation
blocks.zh: 2.1 建议有限责任公司

blocks.en:
Language-model-based recommendation builds on earlier work which formulates recommendation as a text generation task. P5 represents user interactions, item information, and different recommendation tasks in a unified text-to-text framework ( Geng et al., 2022 ) . With the development of instruction-tuned LLMs, researchers began to examine whether a general language model could perform recommendation directly. A common setting presents the user’s history, candidate items, and ranking instruction in natural language, then asks the model to return a ranked list ( Hou et al., 2024b ) . Later studies adapted LLMs more closely to recommendation data and item spaces. TALLRec tunes an LLM
with recommendation instructions for the prediction of user preference ( Bao et al., 2023 ) ; BIGRec generates semantic item representations and maps them to actual items through a two-step grounding procedure ( Bao et al., 2025 ) ; GenRec directly generates target items from textual user and item information ( Ji et al., 2024 ) . Moreover, RecRanker tunes an LLM for pointwise, pairwise, and listwise top- k k ranking tasks ( Luo et al., 2025 ) . LLMs have also been integrated into multi-stage recommendation systems. LlamaRec first retrieves a smaller candidate set with a lightweight sequential recommender and then applies an LLM ranker to those candidates ( Yue et al., 2023 ) . Together, these studies cover several ways of using language models in recommendation tasks, like task-specific tuning, item grounding, direct generation, candidate ranking, and retrieval ranking integration. More recent research has expanded the evaluation beyond average
ranking quality because strong aggregate performance does not guarantee reliable results for every user or candidate set ( Jiang et al., 2025 ) . This broader reliability perspective includes uncertainty and fairness across recommendation cases ( Sah et al., 2026 ) , as well as the sensitivity to preference and presentation biases ( Tang et al., 2026 ) . Building on this reliability
perspective, our study evaluates whether uncertainty signals can identify unreliable issued rankings while keeping the recommender output and candidate order fixed.

blocks.en: 2.2 Uncertainty Quantification
blocks.zh: 2.2 不确定性的量化

blocks.en:
Uncertainty quantification provides signals for assessing how reliable a model’s output is ( Gawlikowski et al., 2023 ) . Probability-based methods summarize
uncertainty through quantities such as maximum confidence, predictive entropy, and the gap between leading candidates ( Gawlikowski et al., 2023 ; Hendrycks and Gimpel, 2016 ; Settles, 2009 ) . Calibration addresses a different question by testing whether the reported confidence matches observed frequencies of correctness ( Guo et al., 2017 ) . Selective prediction examines how prediction risk changes as increasingly uncertain examples are removed ( Geifman and El-Yaniv, 2017 ) . These properties are related, but strong performance on one does not guarantee strong performance on the others. For language models, uncertainty can also be estimated from generated responses. Prior work studied whether a model can assess the correctness of its own answer ( Kadavath et al., 2022 ) while repeated generations reveal how stable its outputs are. Self-consistency measures agreement across sampled outputs ( Wang et al., 2022 ) , and semantic uncertainty groups responses by meaning before measuring their variation ( Kuhn et al., 2023 ) . Recent studies further examine the relationship between sample consistency and confidence calibration ( Lyu et al., 2025 ; Xiao et al., 2025 ) . However, these methods rely on different outputs and sampling procedures, which makes their uncertainty scores difficult to compare under a common
evaluation setup. In recommendation, uncertainty has been used for several purposes. Paliwal et al. (2024) study predictive uncertainty in CTR-based
recommendation through selective prediction, out-of-distribution detection, and active learning. Angelopoulos et al. (2023) construct recommendation sets with finite sample of false-discovery control, and Li et al. (2025) use the list-distribution uncertainty to estimate recommendation performance without relevance labels. For LLM-based
recommendation, Kweon et al. (2025) decompose uncertainty into recommendation and prompt components. Other studies use uncertainty to change the recommendation process. GUIDER adjusts the reranking decisions according to uncertainty ( Xu et al., 2026 ) , and uncertainty-aware generative recommendation incorporates uncertainty into preference optimization and confidence learning ( Fan et al., 2026 ) . Unlike approaches that use uncertainty to modify the recommendation process,
our benchmark evaluates heterogeneous UQ signals after the ranking has been
issued, keeping the candidate order fixed and mapping every method to the same
record-level output contract for direct comparison.

blocks.en: 2.3 Robustness of Recommender Systems
blocks.zh: 2.3 推荐人系统的健全性

blocks.en:
Robustness research examines whether a recommender remains reliable when its
data are sparse, imbalanced, noisy, or perturbed ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) . Sparse user histories make it difficult to represent user preferences accurately ( Adomavicius and Tuzhilin, 2005 ) . Also, popularity
imbalance may reduce the visibility and recommendation quality of tail items ( Abdollahpouri et al., 2019 ) . In LLM-based recommendation, these problems
appear through the textual evidence included in the prompt because missing
user history or item information can change both the resulting ranking and its
uncertainty score. Input perturbations provide a direct way to study this sensitivity. Oh et al. (2022) measure how recommendation lists change after small
perturbations to user interactions. Controlled testing provides a broader
framework for evaluating model behavior. For example, CheckList uses targeted behavioral
tests to reveal failures which the aggregate accuracy may hide ( Ribeiro et al., 2020 ) . Moreover, recent LLM robustness work also examines the model
stability under controlled prompt variations which preserve the original
meaning ( Romanou et al., 2026 ) . These studies suggest that results
from one reference setting may not describe how a model behaves after its
input evidence changes. Recommendation research has also examined which inputs
contribute to uncertainty. Explainable Uncertainty Attribution measures how
individual interactions in a user’s history affect predictive uncertainty in
sequential recommendation ( Balsells-Rodas et al., 2024 ) . Building on controlled robustness testing, our analysis focuses on two
predefined evidence sources, user history and item content, and evaluates
whether changes in UQ responses agree with the NDCG@10 differences associated with the two controls. This scoped evaluation differs from general
source attribution and does not claim causal identification.

blocks.en:
Given a fixed LLM reranking record with a user history, 20 candidate items,
and a parsed base ranking, our benchmark evaluates UQ methods as record-level
monitors of the issued ranking, with the candidate order kept fixed. Each method outputs a scalar uncertainty score aligned to the same base record and may additionally provide paired-control
response scores for user-history and item-content evidence. The two controls are paired at the base-instance level: the same underlying recommendation case is evaluated under full versus truncated user history and under original versus ablated item content. Our benchmark
examines three questions: (1) whether a UQ score can identify an Error@10
case, where the positive item is absent from the fixed top-10 ranking;
(2) whether the relative performance of UQ methods remains stable across
backbones and evaluation conditions; and (3) whether the control-specific UQ responses agree with which source has the larger clipped NDCG@10 difference.

blocks.en: 3.4 UQ Monitoring Signals
blocks.zh: 3.4 UQ 监测信号

blocks.en:
Section 3.3 defines the evaluation targets and metrics
in terms of generic scalar uncertainty scores and control-specific response
scores. We next describe the eight UQ signals used to produce these quantities.
These signals span probability-based confidence, calibration, decomposition,
perturbation sensitivity, and sampling ( Gawlikowski et al., 2023 ; Kweon et al., 2025 ) . The resulting
ranking-level signals may reflect both aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty,
including ambiguity or incompleteness in user or item evidence and sensitivity
to the model, prompt, or sampling procedure. We evaluate their observed
monitoring behavior under a shared protocol without imposing an
aleatoric–epistemic decomposition. All signals monitor the same fixed base
ranking. Detailed score definitions, orientation conventions, and implementation
parameters are provided in Appendix A.3 .

用于模型、即时或取样程序。 我们评价他们的观察

blocks.en:
LabelProb-Max derives uncertainty from the maximum next-token probability over
the valid candidate labels A–T ( Hendrycks and Gimpel, 2016 ) . LabelProb-Entropy measures dispersion over the
same option-label distribution ( Shannon, 1948 ; Settles, 2009 ) , while LabelProb-Margin
measures ambiguity between the two most probable labels ( Scheffer et al., 2001 ; Settles, 2009 ) . Temperature-scaled LabelProb
applies post-hoc scalar calibration to this distribution ( Guo et al., 2017 ) . LabelProb-Top10Mass derives uncertainty from the
probability mass assigned to the fixed base top-10 set, thereby aligning the
probability-mass cutoff with the monitored Error@10 event. Top10Mass combines the option-label distribution from a separate
one-letter prompt with the issued listwise ranking, so it partly measures
cross-elicitation consistency between the two elicitation formats.
Appendix A.12 compares it with teacher-forced
scores reconstructed under the original listwise ranking prompt.

candidate-order variants to separate the recommendation and prompt uncertainty components. Self-consistency draws five stochastic rankings for each record and measures
their top-10 disagreement, following prior work which uses output consistency as uncertainty evidence ( Wang et al., 2022 ; Xiao et al., 2025 ) .

blocks.en:
Perturbation Rank Instability measures how strongly the fixed top-10 set
changes under the constructed user-history and item-content controls,
following perturbation-based behavioral evaluation ( Ribeiro et al., 2016 ; Ribeiro et al., 2020 ) . In addition to its scalar
instability score, the method retains separate user-history and item-content
responses for the paired-control evaluation. Beyond the base ranking, the four LabelProb signals share one forward pass; temperature scaling reuses this pass and adds an offline calibration fit. Decomposed LLM UQ uses five forward passes, self-consistency five sampled generations, and Perturbation Rank Instability 7.3 controlled greedy generations on average. The Llama evaluation reuses the controlled rankings generated for the robustness conditions (Appendix A.14 ).

blocks.en: 5 Conclusion
blocks.zh: 5 结论

blocks.en:
We present a fixed-ranking benchmark for uncertainty quantification in
LLM-based recommendation, where UQ methods monitor the same issued rankings
without changing the candidate order. Across four datasets, the benchmark
evaluates ranking-failure detection, the stability of UQ method performance
across backbones and evaluation conditions, and paired-control response
agreement for user-history and item-content evidence. Our results show that no single UQ ordering is preserved across all settings. Top10Mass achieves the strongest pooled Error@10 detection performance
under several Llama conditions, reflecting effective cutoff-aligned monitoring, while its advantage becomes smaller on the tail-target subset. The same Warm-start evaluation on Qwen produces a different method ordering.
For paired controls, Perturbation Rank Instability provides stronger agreement
with the relative clipped NDCG@10 differences than the scalar UQ signals; simple listwise distances also agree strongly with these clipped differences, supporting source-specific diagnosis. These results
show that UQ quality is task-dependent. A scalar monitor that is effective for ranking-failure detection may not be the most informative for controlled evidence-response agreement. The practical monitoring claim is limited to Error@10 for a single observed positive item. A UQ monitor validated on the target backbone and recommendation
condition can route high-uncertainty requests to a fallback recommender.
Risk–coverage curves on held-out data can guide threshold selection.
Risk@80 and AURC describe ranking errors among retained LLM outputs.
An online A/B test of the complete routing policy would measure
click-through and conversion rates. By holding the issued ranking fixed and aligning
all methods to the same records, our benchmark makes these differences directly
comparable without conflating monitoring quality with reranking behavior.
This separation provides a common basis for evaluating UQ methods across recommendation conditions.
